day.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.
day.readme: My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding. Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve. These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.

Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialized tasks. Skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that's creating documents with your company's brand guidelines, analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows, or automating personal tasks.

day.description: Control your Samsung appliances from Home Assistant over your home network, with no cloud account.
day.readme: Control your Samsung appliances from Home Assistant over your home network, with no cloud account. day.description: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE). A management plane for GPU Kubernetes on bare metal.
day.readme: Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure. NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. week.description: Worktrunk is a CLI for Git worktree management, designed for parallel AI agent workflows
week.readme: Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel. Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches. AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel.

week.description: Turn Claude Code into a full game dev studio, 49 AI agents, 72 workflow skills, and a complete coordination system mirroring real studio hierarchy.
week.readme: Turn a single Claude Code session into a full game development studio. 49 agents. 74 skills. One coordinated AI team. Building a game solo with AI is powerful, but a single chat session has no structure. No one stops you from hardcoding magic numbers, skipping design docs, or writing spaghetti code. There's no QA pass, no design review, no one asking "does this actually fit the game's vision?" Claude Code Game Studios solves this by giving your AI session the structure of a real studio.

week.readme: My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding. Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve. new.readme: asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original.

items.title: Firms barred from running prototype agents locally can hunt preview flaws inside their own AWS
items.connection: On 2026-11-01 Magpie suggested a repo agent run the Cloudflare security-audit skill and file issues for sandbox holes in HTML previews; today Claude Code can run that audit in isolated sessions inside the firm's own AWS account and return fixes as GitHub pull requests, which moves the idea from a prototype on a laptop to something security teams can approve.
items.context: Most enterprises forbid unvetted agents on developer laptops or sending code to outside services
chain: Claude Code now runs remotely in isolated sessions in the customer's AWS account.
The audit skill, which keeps drawing stars, can run inside those sessions, so code never leaves the firm's cloud.
Findings arrive as pull requests, so they enter the normal review and merge path instead of a separate report.
Security teams can schedule the preview-flaw hunt across many repos, and the bottleneck shifts from finding flaws to reviewing PRs.
items.who: AppSec teams at companies that render user HTML (docs tools, email builders, CMS vendors); the security budget pays.
items.variable: Preview sandbox flaws found and fixed per quarter
items.versus: It reuses an approved cloud boundary and the existing PR workflow, instead of buying a separate scanner that cannot propose fixes.
items.smallest_test: Seed a few known sandbox-escape flaws into a copy of one repo with HTML previews, run the skill through Claude Code on AgentCore, and count it a success if a majority of seeded flaws come back as correct, mergeable PRs.
items.disconfirm: The remote sessions miss most seeded flaws, or reviewers reject most of the PRs as wrong or unsafe.

items.title: Biotech labs can qualify a local model on wet-lab tasks before trusting it
items.connection: BioBasicsBench measures agents on 100 everyday wet-lab tasks, and Unsloth's Dynamic V3.1 GGUFs are said to cut Qwen3.8-Flash-Next token use about 50 percent, making a local multimodal candidate fast enough to run the full set on lab hardware.
items.context: Labs often cannot send unpublished experimental data to third-party APIs
chain: Labs now have a yardstick for agents reading raw experimental data.
A local model that uses fewer tokens per answer can run all 100 tasks quickly on a workstation, keeping data in house.
Labs get their own pass or fail score instead of relying on vendor claims.
A passing local model can then handle routine data interpretation without a data-sharing agreement.
items.who: Lab informatics leads at biotechs and CROs; R and D operations would pay.
items.variable: Scientist hours spent on routine data interpretation
items.versus: Sending data to a cloud model raises IP and compliance questions, and adopting a local model untested risks silent errors.
items.smallest_test: Run the quantized Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on BioBasicsBench on one lab workstation and also on a hosted frontier model; success is the local model scoring close enough that scientists would trust it for first-pass reads.
items.disconfirm: The token savings come with accuracy that falls far below hosted models on the benchmark's tasks.

items.title: Consultants can answer the Kimi switch question with free logic tests first
items.connection: Kimi-K3.1-Pro is in three newsletters with 1,586 likes, WeirdML puts it at 9.9 percent and behind Haiku 5.5, and Agents SDK ScriptedResponses lets you test agent logic offline without model calls, so failures can be split into harness bugs and model weakness cheaply.
items.context: Clients ask about whatever model is trending, and swap tests are usually run with no baseline
chain: Hype guarantees clients will ask about switching to Kimi K3.1 Pro.
An independent agentic score already tempers expectations, but it is one run through one provider.
Scripted offline tests prove the client's own tool logic is sound at no model cost, so any later failure points at the model.
Consultants can sell a fixed-price model swap assessment that reuses the same offline suite for every future trending model.
items.who: AI consultancies and internal platform teams; client CTOs pay for the assessment.
items.variable: Cost and time to make a model-swap decision
items.versus: Swapping models directly mixes harness bugs with model gaps, so teams blame the wrong thing and waste spend.
items.smallest_test: Build a ScriptedResponses suite for one client agent, confirm it passes, then run live tasks on Kimi K3.1 Pro and Haiku 5.5; success is a clear recommendation delivered in under a week.
items.disconfirm: Live results on the client's tasks contradict the WeirdML ranking so often that the offline suite plus public score adds no decision value.

items.title: Regulated engineering teams can run QA and release roles as remote PR agents
items.connection: gstack packages 23 Claude Code tools for roles like Release Manager, Doc Engineer and QA, and Claude Code now runs remotely in isolated sessions in your own AWS account returning GitHub PRs, so each role becomes a controlled, reviewable job.
items.context: Banks and insurers require code changes to pass through audited review and stay in approved cloud accounts
chain: Coding agents can now run inside the firm's own AWS account instead of a laptop.
Role-based tools give those sessions defined jobs such as QA passes, release notes and docs updates.
Each role's output is a PR, so existing approval rules and audit trails apply without new process.
Compliance can approve agent roles one at a time, starting with low-risk ones like docs, which makes adoption incremental.
items.who: Platform engineering at banks, insurers and health firms; the engineering productivity budget pays.
items.variable: Engineer hours spent on release notes, docs and QA chores per release
items.versus: Laptop agents fail security review, and a vendor-hosted agent sends code outside the approved boundary.
items.smallest_test: Run gstack's Doc Engineer and Release Manager roles remotely on one service for two release cycles; success is reviewers merging most PRs with minor edits.
items.disconfirm: Reviewers spend more time correcting the role PRs than the chores took by hand.

items.title: Platform teams can serve one distilled agent per workflow on a single partitioned GPU
items.connection: The SageMaker guide produces small students of frontier agent behavior, MIG slices give each student its own hardware-isolated partition, and the llm-d router becomes the single entry point that sends each request to the right slice.
items.context: Frontier API prices make multi-step tool loops expensive at production volume
chain: MIG on SageMaker Inference lets one GPU hold several isolated models instead of one.
Distilled students are small enough that a whole GPU per student wasted most of it, so a slice now fits each workflow's student.
A router in front lets teams add a new workflow-specific student without new hardware or a new endpoint.
Distilling a new narrow agent becomes a routine, cheap project, so teams move many more agent loops off frontier APIs.
items.who: ML platform teams at SaaS firms with several agent features benefit; the product lines whose API bills shrink would fund it.
items.variable: Serving cost per completed agent task
items.versus: Paying frontier prices for every tool loop, or giving each small model a whole GPU, leaves most of the saving unrealized.
items.smallest_test: Distill one high-volume agent workflow, serve it on one MIG slice behind the router next to a second model on another slice, and count it a success if task completion stays within a few points of the frontier model at a clearly lower cost per task.
items.disconfirm: Latency or quality on a shared, partitioned GPU degrades so much under real load that each student needs a whole GPU anyway.

Its 23 Claude Code tools add role-based workflows to the remotely hosted coding agent.

A memory layer that learns from experience adds persistence the semantic-layer grounding lacks across sessions.
Document parsing supplies PDF and office-file context alongside the catalog's certified business definitions.

Patch the Planet connects open source maintainers with responders when coding agents using the security-audit skill uncover critical vulnerabilities.
Code the audit skill generates to probe a finding can execute in an isolated sandbox without leaking credentials.
Turning mixed inputs into enforced constraints adds consistency planning that short 15-second clips lack across a story.
Automatic highlight cutting adds a post-generation editing step to the video the model produces.
Text-to-speech supplies a voice track for generated or edited video clips.
Quantizing the recurrent state shrinks the constant memory of a gated linear-attention model further for smaller hardware.
Document indexing adds a retrieval step for supplying relevant text to Muir's long context.
Soft-token memory summaries address agent context compaction while linear attention handles raw long inputs at constant memory.
Training-free edits offer a way to adapt a trending open 65B model for censorship or sycophancy without retraining.

items.lead: AWS now lets one GPU on its managed inference service serve several models at once, each in its own hardware-isolated slice.
items.body: Teams running small and mid-sized models can size compute to each model instead of paying for a whole GPU per model. That could lower serving cost. The only measurements so far are AWS's own, compared against an older full GPU.

items.lead: Enterprises can now run Claude Code as a remote agent inside their own AWS account.
items.body: Each task runs in an isolated session, and the output comes back as a GitHub pull request for human review. That gives platform and security teams a controlled place to run coding agents without sending work outside their own cloud. The guidance is a how-to post with no cost or throughput figures.

items.lead: Data agents on Google Cloud can now answer from certified business definitions instead of guessing at what a metric means.
items.body: The catalog indexes semantic layers from Looker, dbt MetricFlow and Snowflake automatically and shows them as a visual context graph. For buyers, this targets a common failure where an agent reports the wrong version of a metric. So far there is only a demo video, and no measured accuracy gain.
